blocks.text: Multi-document prompting handles the case where retrieval returns several relevant source documents at once, labeling each one distinctly, resolving conflicting information between them, and managing the combined token budget several documents together consume.

This topic covers clearly labeling multiple documents, handling contradictions and redundancy across them, ordering documents by relevance, managing token budget, and instructing the model to cite which specific document supports each claim.
1. What Multi-Document Prompting Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539584-698320118.png

Multi-document prompting covers the specific challenges that arise once retrieval returns not just one but several relevant pieces of source material for a single query, each needing to be incorporated into the prompt clearly and used correctly.
2. Labeling Each Document Distinctly
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539585-650138380.png

This directly extends the multiple input handling covered in the earlier Input topic, each retrieved document needs its own clear label, Document A, Document B, so the model, and any later citation the model produces, can unambiguously reference which specific source a piece of information actually came from.

code.content:
prompt = f"""
Document A:
{doc_a_text}

Document B:
{doc_b_text}

Answer the question using these documents, and note which document supports each claim.
"""

blocks.text: 3. Handling Conflicting Information Across Documents
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539585-506354163.png

Retrieved documents do not always agree, one source might state a policy detail that another, perhaps outdated, source contradicts, instructing the model explicitly on how to handle this, note the conflict rather than silently picking one, or favor the more recent or more authoritative source if that can be determined, prevents the model from silently resolving a genuine conflict in an unpredictable way.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Situation","Instruction Approach"],"rows":[["Documents agree","Synthesize into one confirmed claim"],["Documents conflict","Explicitly note the conflict rather than silently choosing one side"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Handling Redundant Information Across Documents
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539586-982611401.png

When multiple retrieved documents restate the same underlying fact, instructing the model to synthesize this into one clear statement, rather than repeating the same point several times just because it appeared in multiple sources, keeps the final answer concise and readable.
5. Ordering Documents by Relevance
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539586-921015807.png

This connects to the earlier How LLMs Process Prompts topic, presenting the most relevant retrieved document first, rather than in an arbitrary order, gives it a stronger position of influence in the prompt, most retrieval systems already produce a relevance ranking, worth actually using when constructing the prompt.
6. Managing Token Budget Across Multiple Documents

blocks.alt: Managing Token Budget Across Multiple Documents
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539587-174242167.png

This connects directly to the context window optimization concepts covered in an earlier module, several full length documents can quickly consume a large portion of the available context, prioritizing the most relevant documents, or the most relevant sections within them, keeps the combined content within a reasonable budget.

blocks.title: This is where retrieval quality and prompt construction meet
blocks.content: A prompt construction strategy can only work with whatever documents retrieval actually returns, if retrieval consistently returns too many marginally relevant documents, tightening the retrieval step itself, covered in the separate RAG and Vector Search course, may matter more than prompt level fixes alone.

blocks.text: 7. Citing Which Document Supports Each Claim

blocks.alt: Citing Which Document Supports Each Claim
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473539587-283009596.png

Instructing the model to note which specific labeled document supports each claim it makes gives a reader a way to verify any individual statement directly, this directly previews the source attribution topic covered later in this module, applied here specifically to the multi-document case.
8. A Worked Multi-Document Prompt Example

For a question about a company shipping policy, with three retrieved document excerpts, a well constructed prompt clearly labels each, instructs the model to synthesize consistent information across them, explicitly flag any conflicting detail rather than silently pick one, and cite which document supports each specific claim in the final answer.
9. Multi-Document Prompting and the Rest of This Module

This topic sets up the final two topics in this module directly, answer synthesis prompting covers combining information from multiple documents into one coherent answer in more depth, and source attribution covers citation practices more thoroughly, both building on the multi-document handling covered here.
Worked Example

A developer building a research assistant retrieves three documents for a question, two agreeing on a specific figure and one, an older document, stating a different, outdated figure, without explicit conflict handling instructions, the model silently picks one figure without flagging the discrepancy.

Adding explicit instructions to note conflicting information across documents, and to favor more recent sources when a conflict cannot otherwise be resolved, produces a response that correctly flags the discrepancy and explains which figure is more likely current, giving the user genuinely useful information rather than a silently resolved, potentially wrong answer.
Common Mistakes

items: Not clearly labeling each retrieved document, making it impossible for the model or a citation to reference a specific source
Leaving conflicting information across documents unaddressed, letting the model silently pick one side
Including every retrieved document in full regardless of length, overwhelming the available token budget
Not instructing the model to synthesize redundant information, producing an answer that repeats the same point several times

blocks.text: Practice

Take a question and three short simulated source excerpts, with two agreeing and one containing a conflicting detail, construct a multi-document prompt with clear labels and explicit conflict handling instructions, and test whether the model correctly flags the discrepancy rather than silently resolving it.
Key Takeaway

Multi-document prompting requires clearly labeling each retrieved source, explicitly handling conflicting and redundant information across them, managing the combined token budget, and instructing the model to cite which specific document supports each claim, rather than treating several retrieved sources as one undifferentiated block of text.
